Problem 16[edit]

In a table tennis tournament, every participant played every other participant exactly once. Although there were twice as many right-handed players as left-handed players, the number of games won by left-handed players was more than the number of games won by right-handed players. (There were no ties and no ambidextrous players.) What is the total number of games played?

Solution 8(Pairing) - easiest noncheese[edit]

Case 1: in-group pairing


In every pair where both players use the same hand, the win rate is always \(50\%\). This is because the total number of such pairs is even — any factorial other than the trivial case \(1!\) is even, and \(1\) is insufficient to form a pair. Thus, no player is left out, and in each pair exactly one player wins and one loses, giving a win‑loss ratio of \(1:1\). In other words, this case completely cancels out due to its balanced win‑loss ratio.


Case 2: cross-group pairing


For convenience, let left‑handed players be denoted by \(L\) and right‑handed players by \(R\). The problem gives the ratio \(R : L = 1 : 2\). This means each \(L\) plays \(2L\) times as many games as an \(R\). From this, the total number of cross‑group games is \(2L \times L = 2L^2\).

The problem also states that the ratio of \(L\) wins to \(R\) wins is \(7:5\), so the total number of wins in this case must be divisible by \(5 + 7 = 12\). We therefore require \(2L^2\) to be divisible by \(12\). Simplifying gives \(L^2 \mid 6\). The smallest perfect square divisible by \(6\) is \(\boxed{\textbf{(B)}\ 36}\).

~Twinotter
